basis: The printing heads this quaestio 'VERS. 14.' and it opens '(Vers. 14 et 15.) Issachar bonum desideravit, requiescens inter medios cleros, et videns'. The chapter is Migne's caput, carried from the last one the printing states, and the lemma raises nothing against it.
date_basis: Written at Bethlehem and named in Jerome's own De viris illustribus 135, finished in 393, among the works already published; the preface announces it as the first of a series of Hebrew Questions on the whole of Scripture that he never continued. The early 390s is as close as the evidence held here reaches. The date is the writing, not the 1845 printing and not Vallarsi's 1767 edition.
text: (Vers. 14 et 15.) Issachar bonum desideravit, requiescens inter medios cleros, et videns requiem, quia bona est, et terram, quia pinguis: supposuit humerum suum ad laborandum, et factus est vir agricola. In Hebraeo ita scriptum est: Issachar asinus osseus, recumbens inter terminos, et videns requiem, quia bona est, et terram, quia pulchra est: inclinavit humerum suum ad portandum, et factus est in tributum serviens. Quia supra de Zabulon dixerat, quod maris magni esset littora possessurus, Sidonem quoque et reliquas Phoenicis urbes contingeret; nunc ad mediterraneam provinciam redit, et Issachar, quia juxta Nephthalim, pulcherrimam in Galilaea regionem possessurus est, benedictione sua habitatorem facit. Asinum autem osseum vocat, et humerum ad portandum deditum, quia in labore terrae, et vehendis ad mare oneribus, quae in suis finibus nascebantur, plurimum laboraret, regibus quoque tributa comportans. Aiunt Hebraei, per metaphoram significari, quod Scripturas sanctas die ac nocte meditans, studium suum dederit ad laborandum, et ideo ei omnes tribus serviant, quasi magistro dona portantes.
